deep.reconstruction:
The page has no text, formulas or computation. In the upper part of a light sheet there is only a faint pencil sketch. Two nearly perpendicular straight lines cross, a roughly horizontal axis and a roughly vertical axis. In the upper-right (first) quadrant there are two, possibly three, nested curves. They run from near the vertical axis at the top, bend, and flatten out toward the horizontal axis on the right. In the lower-left (third) quadrant there are one or two corresponding curves running asymptotically toward the negative horizontal axis and the negative vertical axis. The figure is the standard picture of a rectangular hyperbola family x*y = c (c > 0), with branches in opposite quadrants asymptotic to the coordinate axes.

The lower part of the image is the black background beneath a folded or shorter sheet. The right edge shows a sliver of an adjacent leaf with illegible ink traces.

Interpretation (mine, uncertain): in the context of the bundle 'R.Ellipsoid' (Riemann's 1861 work on the motion of a homogeneous fluid ellipsoid, with velocity fields linear in the coordinates), such curves are what one gets as streamlines or particle paths of a planar linear flow u = a*x, v = -a*y. That flow is a pure strain about a stagnation point; its trajectories satisfy x*y = const. The nested curves would then be several streamlines, i.e. different values of the constant. They could equally be a generic doodle of hyperbolas or a quick illustration of asymptotic behaviour.

The next leaf contains Riemann's draft referee report on the Göttingen mathematical prize question on fluid motion in Lagrangian coordinates. The essay bears the motto 'Tanto uberiores sunt notae, quanto magis exprimunt rerum relationes'; this is presumably Hermann Hankel's 1861 prize essay. So the sketch may also be connected to thinking about that essay. No derivation can be reconstructed from this page.

results.what: Pencil sketch of a family of rectangular hyperbolas x*y = c in the first and third quadrants, asymptotic to the axes (possibly streamlines of a planar linear strain flow near a stagnation point)
results.modern_name: Rectangular hyperbola / streamlines of a hyperbolic (pure strain) stagnation-point flow
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Apollonius for hyperbolas; stagnation-point flow standard in 19th-century hydrodynamics)

deep.surprise_reason: The page has only an unlabelled sketch of hyperbola-like curves with their asymptotes. It contains no mathematical content beyond an elementary figure.

The branch y = c/x approaches the horizontal axis asymptotically (limit 0).
